topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Reflection is a printed-diagram question near the front of the paper. Summer 2023 Foundation Q1 was 6 marks: two image properties [2] and a ray diagram with the normal, the reflected ray, the arrow and an angle [4]. Summer 2024 Foundation Q2 gave [3] for the arrow, the angle and the normal and [4] for the image properties. Summer 2024 Higher Q6(c) added a second mirror for [4]. Booklet B sets the ray-tracing practical as a banded question.
mustMemorise: The normal is a line at right angles to the mirror at the point where the ray lands
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal
An angle printed to the mirror surface must be subtracted from 90° first
The image in a plane mirror is the same size as the object, upright, laterally inverted and virtual
The mirror sits exactly halfway between the object and its image
Two mirrors at right angles: the two angles of incidence add up to 90°
Every ray on a diagram carries an arrow showing which way the light travels
notOnThisSpec: Curved mirrors of any kind, concave or convex
Total internal reflection, critical angle and optical fibres
Diffuse reflection from a rough surface as a named term
Snell's law and refractive index (refraction itself is outcome 2.2.3 onwards)
The periscope or the kaleidoscope as required constructions

note.title: Reflection in a plane mirror
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal
The normal is at right angles to the mirror, so an angle printed to the surface is 90° minus the angle of incidence
The image is the same size, upright, laterally inverted, virtual, and as far behind as the object is in front

notOnThisSpec: Total internal reflection and critical angle

mustBeAbleTo: Draw and label the normal at the point where a ray meets a mirror
State the law of reflection and say which line both angles are measured from
Find the angle of reflection from a given angle of incidence
Turn an angle printed to the mirror surface into an angle of incidence
Complete a ray diagram with the reflected ray at the correct angle and an arrow on it
List the properties of the image seen in a plane mirror, using the full phrase laterally inverted
Work out the distance from an object to its image in a plane mirror
Handle two mirrors set at right angles, taking a new normal at the second one
Describe a ray-tracing investigation, naming the ray box and the protractor
sheet.howExamined: P2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. Reflection sits near the front of the paper as a printed diagram with [1] per feature: the normal labelled, the reflected ray drawn by eye, the arrow on it, and an angle stated. Image properties come as a tick list worth [3] or [4], where the listing rule cancels contradictory ticks. Higher Tier adds a second mirror. Unit 7 Physics Booklet B sets the ray-tracing practical, and has used it for the 6-mark banded question.
traps: Copying an angle printed to the mirror surface as the angle of incidence (Summer 2025 U7 Physics Booklet B Q4)
Leaving the arrow off the reflected ray, or pointing it at the mirror (Summer 2023 P2 F Q1; Summer 2024 P2 F Q2)
Writing inverted where the property is laterally inverted (Summer 2023 P2 H Q5)
Ticking two contradictory properties, such as real and virtual, so both cancel (Summer 2023 P2 F Q1)
Repeating a property the question has already given you in the stem (Summer 2023 P2 H Q5)
Answering 90° when the ray arrives along the normal, where both angles are 0° (Summer 2023 P2 H Q5)
Reusing the first angle of incidence at a second mirror (Summer 2024 P2 H Q6)
Giving the image distance when the question asks for the distance from object to image
Omitting the normal altogether from a diagram (Summer 2025 P2 H Q8)

noteBlocks.lede: A flat mirror shows you standing behind it, the same size and the same way up, with your left hand where your right one should be. Nothing is really back there. One rule and one construction line explain all of it.
can: Draw the normal on any mirror diagram and measure both angles from it
Use angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, even from a surface angle
List what the image in a flat mirror looks like, and work out where it is

noteBlocks.md: Look into a flat mirror and you see yourself standing behind it, the same size, the same way up — but with your left hand where your right should be. Nothing is really back there. This topic explains how a mirror does that.

noteBlocks.md:
The ray arriving is the **incident ray**; the ray leaving is the **reflected ray**. Where they meet the mirror you draw the **normal**: a line at **right angles to the mirror**.
The rule is short — the **angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection** — and both angles sit between a ray and the normal.

noteBlocks.prompt: A ray hits a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 48°. What is the angle of reflection, in degrees?
noteBlocks.explain: 48°. The two angles are equal, so there is nothing to work out once you have the angle of incidence.

noteBlocks.md:
A diagram will sometimes mark the angle **between the ray and the mirror surface**. That is not the angle of incidence.
The mirror and the normal are at right angles, so the two angles add to 90°. Here the printed angle is 25°, so the angle of incidence is 90° − 25° = 65°.

noteBlocks.title: Why the normal, and not the mirror?
noteBlocks.md: Because the normal is the one line that behaves the same way for every surface, flat or curved. Measuring from the normal lets the same rule describe a flat mirror, a curved mirror and, later, refraction through glass. Draw the normal first and every angle question in optics becomes the same question.

noteBlocks.prompt: A ray meets a mirror at 30° to the mirror surface. What is the angle of incidence, in degrees?
noteBlocks.explain: 90° − 30° = 60°. Draw the normal, then subtract from 90°.

noteBlocks.md:
Two rays leave the object, reflect, and enter your eye. Your brain assumes light travelled in straight lines all the way, so it traces them back to a point **behind** the mirror. That point is the **image**.
No light ever reaches it, so the image is **virtual**. It is the **same size** as the object, it is **upright**, and the mirror sits exactly **halfway** between it and the object.

noteBlocks.md:
A ray hits mirror A with an angle of incidence of 62°. Find its angle of incidence at mirror B.
**Step 1** — at mirror A, $i = r$, so the ray leaves at 62° to A's normal.
**Step 2** — mirror B is at right angles to A, so B's normal is at right angles to A's normal.
**Step 3** — the ray therefore makes 90° − 62° = 28° with B's normal.
**Answer** — the angle of incidence at mirror B is 28°.

items.skill: Prerequisite: light travels in straight lines

options.feedback: That is why a ruler is the right tool for joining the marks in a ray-tracing experiment.

options.feedback: A protractor, read to the nearest degree. Examiners expect it to be named in a practical answer.
A ruler measures a length. Angles need a protractor.
A set square draws a right angle, which is useful for the normal, but it does not measure an angle of your choice.

options.feedback: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Nothing else to do.

Nothing is halved in reflection. The two angles are simply equal.
The angle of reflection is 0° only when the ray arrives along the normal itself.

options.feedback: 90° − 20°. The normal is at right angles to the mirror, so the two angles add to 90°.
That is the printed angle, measured from the mirror. Summer 2025 Booklet B examiners reported a diagram marked this way costing many candidates the mark.
90° is the angle between the mirror and the normal, not the angle the ray makes with either.

options.feedback: And the same size as the object, with the mirror exactly halfway between the two.

options.text: real, inverted and smaller than the object
options.feedback: Three properties, three errors. A plane-mirror image is virtual, upright and the same size.

options.feedback: The mirror sits exactly halfway between the object and its image.
That is the whole distance from the object to the image. The part behind the mirror is 8 cm.
Nothing is halved. The mirror sits exactly halfway between the object and the image, so both distances are equal.

scheme.examinerNote: The mirror sits exactly halfway between the object and its image.

parts.workedSolution: The mirror sits exactly halfway between the object and its image, so the image appears 12 cm behind the mirror.

parts.stem:
A gymnast stands 12 cm in front of a plane mirror.
Calculate the distance between the gymnast and her image.

scheme.for: the image is 12 cm behind the mirror

hints: Find where the image is first, then measure from the gymnast to it.
The gymnast and the image are on opposite sides of the mirror.
parts.workedSolution: The image lies as far behind the mirror as the gymnast is in front, so it is 12 cm behind. The gymnast is 12 cm in front, and the two distances are on opposite sides of the mirror, so the total distance between her and her image is 12 + 12 = 24 cm.

commonErrors.feedback: That is how far the image is behind the mirror. The question asks for the gap between the gymnast and her image, which spans the mirror, so add the two equal distances: 24 cm.

parts.stem:
She then steps 4 cm closer to the mirror.
Calculate the new distance between the gymnast and her image.

scheme.for: she is now 12 − 4 = 8 cm in front

hints: Work out her new distance from the mirror first.
The image moves too, by the same amount, in the opposite direction.
parts.workedSolution: She is now 12 − 4 = 8 cm in front of the mirror, so her image is 8 cm behind it. The distance between them is 8 × 2 = 16 cm. Moving 4 cm closer shortens the gap by twice that, because the image moves as well.

commonErrors.feedback: The step was subtracted once. Both the gymnast and her image move 4 cm towards the mirror, so the gap closes by 8 cm, leaving 16 cm.

parts.stem:
Two plane mirrors are fixed at right angles to each other. A ray of light strikes mirror A with an angle of incidence of 62°.
State the angle of reflection where that ray leaves mirror A.
hints: The law of reflection applies at every mirror, every time.
parts.workedSolution: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, so the ray leaves mirror A at 62° to the normal at A.

parts.stem: Calculate the angle of incidence where the ray then meets mirror B.

scheme.for: the normals at the two mirrors are at right angles, so the two angles of incidence add to 90°

hints: Mark the normal at mirror B: it is at right angles to mirror B, so it is parallel to mirror A.
The two angles of incidence in this arrangement always add up to 90°.
parts.workedSolution: Mirror B is at right angles to mirror A, so the normal at B is at right angles to the normal at A. The ray makes 62° with the first normal, so it makes 90° − 62° = 28° with the second. The angle of incidence at mirror B is 28°.

commonErrors.feedback: The first angle has been carried straight over. The second mirror has its own normal, at right angles to the first, so the angles of incidence add to 90°: the answer is 28°. Summer 2024 examiners reported that only the most able candidates managed this step.

parts.stem: State the angle of reflection where the ray leaves mirror B.
hints: Same law, second mirror.
parts.workedSolution: The law of reflection applies again, so the angle of reflection at mirror B is 28°.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the angle at mirror A. At mirror B the angle of incidence is 28°, so the angle of reflection there is 28° too.

parts.stem: Explain why the angle of incidence at mirror B is different from the angle of incidence at mirror A.

accepted: the two mirrors are at right angles, so their normals are at right angles and the two angles of incidence add up to 90 degrees

scheme.for: each mirror has its own normal, drawn at right angles to that mirror
the mirrors are at right angles, so the two normals are too, and the angles of incidence add to 90°

hints: Each mirror gets its own normal. Where are the two normals pointing?
parts.workedSolution: Every angle in reflection is measured from the normal of the mirror it strikes, and each mirror has its own normal at right angles to itself. Because the two mirrors are at right angles, the two normals are at right angles as well, so the angle the ray makes with one normal and the angle it makes with the other must add up to 90°.

pattern.regex: measured from the (mirror|surface)|angle to the mirror

commonErrors.feedback: The explanation has to be about the normals, not the mirrors themselves. Draw a normal at each mirror: they are at right angles to each other, which is why the two angles of incidence add to 90°.

context.setting: A practical write-up for a class investigating a plane mirror

parts.stem:
A class is asked to investigate how light is reflected by a plane mirror, using ray tracing.
Describe how they should carry out the investigation, and describe the image they would see in the mirror.
Your written communication is marked here as well: answer in full sentences, in a sensible order, using the specification's own scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: stand the plane mirror upright on a sheet of paper and draw a line along its back
use a ray box (or a lamp with a narrow slit) to send a single narrow ray at the mirror
draw the normal at right angles to the mirror where the ray meets it
mark the incident and reflected rays with crosses or pins and join each pair with a ruler
measure both angles from the normal with a protractor: the one before the ray lands and the one after it leaves
repeat for several different angles of incidence and compare the pairs
the two angles are equal every time, and the image is upright, virtual, laterally inverted and the same size as the object, with the mirror exactly halfway between object and image

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Apparatus, method, measurement, repeat, result, then the image. That is six or seven points.
Name the ray box and the protractor: Booklet B examiners have reported both being left out.
parts.workedSolution: Stand the plane mirror upright on a sheet of paper and draw a line along the back of it to record where it was. Use a ray box with a narrow slit to send a single ray of light at the mirror, and mark on the paper where the ray meets the mirror. Draw the normal at that point, at right angles to the mirror line, using a set square. Mark the path of the incident ray and the path of the reflected ray with two crosses each, take the mirror away and join the crosses with a ruler. Measure both angles from the normal with a protractor, the one before the ray lands and the one after it leaves, and repeat for several different angles. Every pair of angles is equal. Looking into the mirror, the image is upright, virtual, laterally inverted and the same size as the object, and the mirror sits exactly halfway between it and the object.

pattern.regex: measured from the (mirror|surface)|angles? to the mirror

commonErrors.feedback: The account measures angles from the mirror. Both angles are measured from the normal, and drawing that normal is one of the marking points. Booklet B examiners have reported the normal being the mark candidates most often miss here.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked: 'A diagram shows a ray of light meeting a plane mirror at 30° to the mirror surface. State the angle of reflection. [2]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
So the angle of reflection is 30°.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 is the law of reflection, stated correctly. The trouble is line 1: the 30° printed on the diagram is measured from the mirror, and every angle in reflection is measured from the normal. The normal is at right angles to the mirror, so the angle of incidence is 90° − 30° = 60°.
correction: Draw the normal at right angles to the mirror where the ray lands.
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, so the angle of reflection is 60°.
findTheMistake.feedback: No marks, and only one line needed changing. Both marks here are for the numbers, so the correct law in line 2 earns nothing on its own. Summer 2025 Booklet B examiners reported that including an angle to the surface on a diagram made many candidates forfeit the mark. Draw the normal first, every time, and the subtraction becomes obvious.

prompts.prompt: State the law of reflection, and say what both angles are measured from.
prompts.answer: The angle of reflection always equals the angle of incidence. Both are measured from the normal, the line at right angles to the mirror at the point where the ray lands.

prompts.prompt: A diagram marks 20° between a ray and the mirror surface. What is the angle of incidence, and why?
prompts.answer: 70°, because the angle of incidence is measured from the normal and the normal is at right angles to the mirror, so the two angles add up to 90°.

prompts.prompt: List the five properties of the image formed in a plane mirror.
prompts.answer: The image is upright, virtual, laterally inverted and the same size as the object, with the mirror exactly halfway between the object in front and the image behind.

prompts.prompt: Why is 'inverted' not enough when describing the image in a plane mirror?
prompts.answer: Inverted on its own means upside down, and a plane-mirror image is upright. The property is laterally inverted: left and right are swapped over.

prompts.prompt: What is the first line you draw on any reflection diagram, and where does it go?
prompts.answer: The normal: a dashed line at right angles to the mirror, at the exact point where the ray meets it.

prompts.prompt: Two plane mirrors are fixed at right angles. A ray hits the first with an angle of incidence of 55°. What is the angle of incidence at the second?
prompts.answer: 35°, because the two normals are at right angles to each other, so the two angles of incidence add up to 90°.
